restorationist.church:
Restorationist Christians think of the church as the body of Christ, a people called out by God, and they look to the New Testament as the pattern for its life. Many hold that the church should be identified by biblical names, such as the church of Christ, and by biblical practices rather than by later creeds or traditions.

The Restorationist family is broad, and its members differ on many points. Some see many Christian communions as sharing one body in Christ, while others hold that only their own fellowship is the true church. What they share is the desire to be simply the New Testament church, and to let Scripture rather than denominational history shape the church's doctrine, worship and organization.
restorationist.great_apostasy:
Many Restorationists teach that after the time of the apostles the church gradually departed from the teaching and practice of the New Testament, a departure often described as the apostasy or the falling away. They point to biblical warnings about false teachers and to what they see as later additions to doctrine and worship.

Restorationists differ widely about how complete this departure was. Some, such as those in the Stone-Campbell tradition, generally hold that the church never entirely ceased to exist and needed reformation and return to the Bible. Others teach that true authority or truth was lost altogether and had to be restored by God. Many other Christians disagree with the idea of a complete apostasy, and Restorationists are aware of this disagreement.
restorationist.restoration:
Restorationists share the aim of restoring the church to its New Testament pattern, in teaching, worship, names and organization. Their method is to set aside later traditions and human creeds and to go back to the Bible, asking what the first Christians believed and did.

Different Restorationist movements have carried this out in different ways. Some emphasize a return to New Testament practice through careful study, others emphasize that God himself has restored lost authority, teachings or offices. The result is a family of quite different churches, all sharing the conviction that Christian unity and faithfulness require going back to the source, and that the church of the first century is still the model.
restorationist.true_church_claim:
Many Restorationists say that they are not a denomination, but simply the New Testament church, and that they claim no name other than the biblical names for the church. For them this is a statement about faithfulness to Scripture more than a claim to superiority.

Restorationists do not agree among themselves on what this implies for other Christians. Some acknowledge that Christians exist in all churches, and hope for unity around the Bible. Others hold that only their own fellowship truly follows the New Testament pattern, and treat other churches as departing from it. Most other Christians hear the claim as exclusive, and Restorationists who make it usually say that it is meant as an invitation to return to the Bible together.
